title: Louviers Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Louviers wells have a 351-foot median depth, with typical finished-well costs of $23,600-$36,600.
h1: Louviers, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land in Louviers means treating the well as part of the property, not as an afterthought. Records within 5 miles show 2,632 permitted wells, with 1,273 recorded as constructed. Of the wells reporting depth, the median is 351 feet. Reported yields are generally workable, but the local records do not describe every well, and a permit file is not a substitute for a current flow test.

Louviers sits in a Denver Basin setting with sedimentary bedrock and a mix of Denver, Arapahoe, and unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers. Nearby Sterling Ranch, Sedalia, and Roxborough Park can provide useful comparison points, but the lot you are buying still needs its own records, site review, and well inspection.

sections.heading: How deep are Louviers wells?
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Louviers is 351 feet. The middle half runs from 75 to 580 feet, meaning many nearby wells fall across a broad drilling range. A bid based only on the median can miss the local spread: one lot may reach water much shallower, while another may require several hundred additional feet.

The depth mix reinforces that point. Twenty-eight percent of reported wells are under 100 feet, 16% fall from 100 to 300 feet, 32% from 300 to 600 feet, and 24% are deeper than 600 feet. The 90th-percentile depth is 932 feet, with the deepest record at 2,668 feet. Denver Basin sedimentary formations, aquifer choice, bedrock, and the specific parcel all affect the driller's final depth.

sections.heading: What yield can a Louviers well produce?
sections.html:
Reported pump yields have a 12.0 gallons-per-minute median, with the middle half between 10.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. That is a stronger reported range than many buyers expect from a rural well, but it is not a guarantee for an untested property. Only 792 wells in the records report a pump yield.

Sixty-three percent of reported wells produce from 5 to 15 gallons per minute, while 35% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Two percent fall from 1 to 5 gallons per minute, and none are listed under 1 gallon per minute. Ask for the well completion report and a current test. Storage tanks can help manage household demand, but they do not turn a low-producing well into a high-producing one. Exempt household-use wells are generally limited to 35 gallons per minute.

sections.heading: Is the water table dropping around Louviers?
sections.html:
Reported static water levels show water below the ground surface at a 242-foot median, with the middle half from 131 to 358 feet. This is the depth to water when the well is at rest, not the total drilled depth. A pump may sit deeper, and the water level can change after pumping or during dry conditions.

The decade series does not show a simple, continuous decline. The median was 207 feet below surface in the 1980s, 284 feet in the 2010s, and 260 feet in the 2020s. That suggests deeper measured water levels in the later records than in the 1980s, followed by some improvement in the 2020s, but only 90 wells report a static water level. Use the trend as context, not as a parcel-specific prediction.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Louviers, and when?
sections.html:
Permit history is long and concentrated in several periods. Records show 37 permits from the 1950s, 50 in the 1960s, 255 in the 1970s, 309 in the 1980s, 616 in the 1990s, 599 in the 2000s, 276 in the 2010s, and 77 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025, so this is not an area with only legacy wells.

Hier Drilling Co Inc, listed with Hier, Bruce A., appears most often with 607 records. Authorized, listed with Pe, Pg, appears on 227, and Hier Drilling Co., listed with Hier, Peter J., appears on 226. Those records identify who worked in the area, not who is available today or who will provide the best bid. Verify licensing, insurance, references, and the proposed casing and grout details before hiring.

sections.heading: What does a new well cost in Louviers?
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot. Applying that to the 351-foot median depth produces an estimated drilled-hole cost of about $17,600 to $24,600. That is only the hole. It does not cover the complete water system or every site condition.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $23,600 to $36,600 at the median depth. A deeper-than-median result can push the price higher, and the 90th-percentile depth of 932 feet shows why an open-ended drilling allowance matters. Get bids that state the assumed depth, casing, grout, pump equipment, electrical run, trench length, testing, and what happens if the hole is dry or produces less than expected.

sections.heading: What risks should Louviers buyers check?
sections.html:
Low yield is not the leading pattern in the reported records, but incomplete reporting matters: only 792 wells list a pump yield, and only 90 list a static water level. A dry hole, an inadequate production rate, or a failed pump can still make one parcel expensive. Fractured-bedrock conditions can also be unpredictable, even where nearby wells look favorable.

Water quality deserves a separate review. Within about 10 miles are 77 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 20 historic mine features, and 8 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped sites do not prove contamination at a particular home. Test the existing well for common household contaminants and any site-specific concerns identified by the records. Confirm septic setbacks, soil suitability, legal access for drilling, building envelopes, and the location of the well relative to septic systems and property boundaries.

sections.heading: How should you buy or build on a Louviers lot?
sections.html:
Start with the Colorado Division of Water Resources permit file, then compare completed wells near the parcel rather than relying on a regional average. Records from Sterling Ranch, Sedalia, Roxborough Park, Highlands Ranch, Castle Pines Village, and Castle Pines can help establish context, but geology can change over a short distance. Check the well's permitted use, aquifer designation, depth, yield, static level, pump information, and test history.

For a vacant lot, make the well plan part of due diligence before closing. Have a driller review access, rig setup, likely depth, and the cost if drilling goes deeper. Confirm the intended household use, septic location, electrical route, storage needs, and any augmentation-plan requirements in an over-appropriated basin. For an existing home, inspect the pump and pressure system, test the water, and make the sale contingent on documents you can verify.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Louviers, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Louviers is 351 feet. The middle half runs from 75 to 580 feet, while the 90th-percentile depth is 932 feet. About 24% of reported wells are deeper than 600 feet, so a buyer should budget for variation rather than assume every lot will match the median.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Louviers?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50-$70 per foot. At the 351-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $17,600-$24,600. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $23,600-$36,600. A deeper hole, difficult access, or added site work can increase the bid.

faq.q: How much water does a well produce in Louviers?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a 12.0-gpm median, with the middle half from 10.0 to 15.0 gpm. Sixty-three percent of reported wells produce from 5 to 15 gpm, and 35% report more than 15 gpm. These figures cover only 792 records, so obtain a current flow test for the specific property.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Louviers, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from depth or yield. Within about 10 miles, records map 77 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 20 historic mine features, and 8 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those locations do not establish contamination at your property. Test the well for household contaminants and investigate site-specific concerns before buying.

faq.q: Are Louviers well depths getting deeper?
faq.a: The reported median static water level was 207 feet below surface in the 1980s, 284 feet in the 2010s, and 260 feet in the 2020s. That does not show a simple continuous decline, and only 90 wells report static levels. Treat the series as regional context, then inspect the specific well's current level and pumping behavior.
